<div class="markdown"><p>The task stayed fixed in Chapters 1–3; in this chapter it changes. A learner that stores head counts to answer the coin question is now asked for the longest run of heads. Chapter 2 showed that the count cannot answer this question.</p><p>We ask two questions. How can a learner tell that its representation has become insufficient, rather than that its decoder needs more training? And when it revises the representation, what should it change to?</p><p>The paper makes the first point in general: If a distinction that the task needs is missing from the current representation, no amount of optimisation within that representation can recover it. The fix has to add the distinction.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="The-model-and-the-tasks">The model and the tasks</h2><p>The coin model and the two tasks are the same as in Chapters 1–3.</p></div>

```julia
coin_flip(i, ω) =
    (i ~ Bernoulli(is_fair_coin(ω) ? fair_weight : trick_weight))(ω)
```

```julia
flip_sequence(n) = Variable(ω -> [coin_flip(i, ω) for i in 1:n])
```

```julia
show_sequence(sequence) = join(ifelse.(sequence, "H", "T"))
```

```julia
function is_fair_posterior(sequence)
    likelihood(weight) = prod(flip ? weight : 1 - weight for flip in sequence)
    fair_mass = is_fair_prior * likelihood(fair_weight)
    trick_mass = (1 - is_fair_prior) * likelihood(trick_weight)
    fair_mass / (fair_mass + trick_mass)
end
```

```julia
function longest_head_run(sequence)
    longest = 0
    current = 0
    for s in sequence
        current = s ? current + 1 : 0
        longest = max(longest, current)
    end
    longest
end
```

```julia
all_boolean_sequences(n) = [
    [isone((mask >> i) & 1) for i in 0:n-1]
    for mask in 0:(2^n - 1)
]
```

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="A-library-of-representations">A library of representations</h2><p>The learner can choose among four representations:</p><ul><li><p><code>count</code> is the <code>(flips, heads)</code> pair from Chapter 1.</p></li><li><p><code>count_and_run</code> adds the longest head run as an extra coordinate.</p></li><li><p><code>reversal_form</code> is the reversal canonical form from Chapter 3: the alphabetically first of the sequence and its mirror image.</p></li><li><p><code>full_sequence</code> keeps every flip in order.</p></li></ul></div>

```julia
count_representation(s) = (flips = length(s), heads = count(identity, s))
```

```julia
count_and_run(s) = (flips = length(s), heads = count(identity, s),
                    longest_run = longest_head_run(s))
```

```julia
reversal_form(s) = min(show_sequence(s), show_sequence(reverse(s)))
```

```julia
full_sequence(s) = show_sequence(s)
```

```julia
representation_library = [
    :count => count_representation,
    :count_and_run => count_and_run,
    :reversal_form => reversal_form,

]
```

<div class="markdown"><p>For four flips the representations have 5, 7, 10 and 16 distinct coordinates.</p><p>The four form a chain in which each one keeps every distinction the previous one keeps and adds more: two sequences that share a <code>reversal_form</code> also share a <code>count_and_run</code>, and two that share a <code>count_and_run</code> also share a <code>count</code>. <code>refines</code> checks this ordering over every sequence.</p></div>

```julia
refines(finer, coarser, n) = all(
    coarser(s) == coarser(t)
    for s in all_boolean_sequences(n) for t in all_boolean_sequences(n)
    if finer(s) == finer(t))
```

<div class="markdown"><p><code>count_and_run</code> may look like cheating, because it stores the answer to the new task directly. It <em>expands</em> the representation: it adds an axis that the old one lacked. Whether it is a good revision depends on the tasks that come next.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Insufficient-or-badly-tuned?">Insufficient or badly tuned?</h2><p>A learner that keeps the count can still change its decoder, which is a table from count coordinates to answers. The best table answers each coordinate with the most common answer among the training sequences that map to it. <code>fit_decoder</code> builds that table from training data, and <code>test_error</code> measures how often it is wrong on fresh sequences. A coordinate that never appeared in training counts as an error.</p></div>

```julia
function fit_decoder(representation, training, task)
    table = Dict{Any, Dict{Any, Int}}()
    for s in training
        answers = get!(table, representation(s), Dict{Any, Int}())
        answers[task(s)] = get(answers, task(s), 0) + 1
    end
    Dict(key => first(argmax(last, collect(answers))) for (key, answers) in table)
end
```

```julia
test_error(representation, decoder, test, task) =
    mean(get(decoder, representation(s), missing) !== task(s) for s in test)
```

<div class="markdown"><p>As the training set grows, the error of every representation except <code>count</code> falls towards zero. The error of <code>count</code> levels off at about 0.27, however much data it sees.</p><p>The next cell computes that floor exactly. For each coordinate, the best possible decoder picks the answer with the most probability; whatever probability is left over in that class is error that no table can avoid.</p></div>

```julia
function sequence_probability(s)
    n, k = length(s), count(identity, s)
    is_fair_prior * fair_weight^k * (1 - fair_weight)^(n - k) +
        (1 - is_fair_prior) * trick_weight^k * (1 - trick_weight)^(n - k)
end
```

```julia
function best_possible_error(representation, task, n)
    mass = Dict{Any, Dict{Any, Float64}}()
    for s in all_boolean_sequences(n)
        answers = get!(mass, representation(s), Dict{Any, Float64}())
        answers[task(s)] = get(answers, task(s), 0.0) + sequence_probability(s)
    end
    sum(sum(values(a)) - maximum(values(a)) for a in values(mass))
end
```

```julia
[(representation = name,
  best_possible_error = best_possible_error(r, longest_head_run, sequence_length))
 for (name, r) in representation_library]
```

<div class="markdown"><p><code>count</code> has an error floor of about 0.27; the other representations have none. The floor comes from the classes with two and three heads. In each, half the sequences have one longest run and half have another, and they are equally likely under both coins.</p><p>This floor is the diagnostic: more data and better decoding only move <code>count</code> towards it. When the error stays above zero after the decoder has converged, the problem is the representation, not the tuning. Removing the floor requires moving up the chain to a representation that separates the sequences <code>count</code> merges.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Revising-the-representation">Revising the representation</h2><p>We now infer which representation to use, in the same way as Chapter 3. The prior favours representations with fewer coordinates, and we condition on consistency with labelled examples.</p><p>The examples now come from a <em>stream of tasks</em>. The learner wants a single representation that serves every task it has seen so far. A third task asks whether the first flip is a head.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><p>Each example records its task, a sequence and the answer. A representation is consistent when no two examples from the same task share a coordinate but have different answers.</p></div>

```julia
same_answer(a, b) = a isa AbstractFloat ? isapprox(a, b) : a == b
```

```julia
function is_consistent(representation, examples)
    answers = Dict{Any, Any}()
    for (task_name, sequence, answer) in examples
        key = (task_name, representation(sequence))
        if haskey(answers, key)
            same_answer(answers[key], answer) || return false
        else
            answers[key] = answer
        end
    end
    true
end
```

<div class="markdown"><p>Read the table one row at a time.</p><ol><li><p>After the fair-coin task, every representation is consistent, so the posterior matches the prior and <code>count</code> is most probable.</p></li><li><p>After the longest-run task, <code>count</code> usually drops to zero: some pair of examples has the same head count but different runs. <code>count_and_run</code> is now the cheapest consistent choice.</p></li><li><p>After the first-flip task, <code>count_and_run</code> and <code>reversal_form</code> usually drop to zero too, and only <code>full_sequence</code> remains.</p></li></ol><p>The examples are random, so a stage can fail to rule out a representation. If a row looks different, rerun <code>task_examples</code> or raise <code>examples_per_task</code>.</p><p>A conflict triggered each revision, and a conflict is the example-level version of the error floor above. A learner that revises its representation therefore has several distinct jobs: detect a mismatch, decide whether better tuning within the current representation could fix it, and propose a new representation when it cannot.</p><p>As in Chapter 3, this learner chooses from a library we supplied. Every move here is along a chain we built in advance. A learner that constructs the next representation itself faces a much harder search.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Which-revision-carries-over?">Which revision carries over?</h2><p>At stage 2, <code>count_and_run</code> and <code>reversal_form</code> both fix the failure, and the prior prefers <code>count_and_run</code> because it is smaller. The next cell checks, over every sequence, which representations would suffice for other tasks the learner might meet next.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><p><code>count_and_run</code> answers the task it was built for and nothing else on this list. <code>reversal_form</code> also answers the longest tail run and the number of runs. Neither answers the first-flip question, which needs the order itself.</p><p>Part of this result is unsurprising: <code>reversal_form</code> is finer, and <code>full_sequence</code>, the finest, answers everything. The interesting point is <em>why</em><code>reversal_form</code> stops where it does. It groups a sequence only with its mirror image, and reversal preserves every run. So it discards exactly the distinctions that no run-based task needs, and keeps the rest. <code>count_and_run</code> was built from one answer and has no such reason to carry over. A representation derived from a transformation that the tasks respect tends to transfer to related tasks; one built by storing an answer does not.</p><p>The best revision therefore depends on which tasks come next, and a learner rarely knows that in advance. When tasks keep changing, no single representation stays best, so revising a representation is never finished.</p><h2 id="Discussion">Discussion</h2><p>Use <code>HHHT</code> and <code>HTHH</code>. What observation first tells you that <code>count</code> has become insufficient for the longest run? Would that observation also tell you which representation to switch to?</p><p>Reorder <code>task_stream</code> so that the first-flip task comes second. Which representations survive each stage now? Does the learner end in the same place?</p><p>Chapter 3 derived <code>reversal_form</code> from a generator, while we built <code>count_and_run</code> by adding an answer. Which kind of revision would you expect to transfer better to a new domain? Chapter 5 takes up that question.</p></div>
